name: WE-061 Lanvik App-Based Work Act 2027 (loop_r2 seed)

unclear.text: Waiting time: is time logged in and waiting for a request time during which the worker is required by the network company to remain available (section 5(2))?
readings: U1-a: no; a worker may log off at will, so only time on a trip, and any shift a company schedules, is engaged time
U1-b: yes; the apps reduce the priority of workers who decline requests, so all logged-in time is engaged time

a1.text: The Act is enforced: audits and private suits with double damages make treating workers as contractors without a valid agreement costly.

a2.text: Each company elects to offer contractor agreements.

a3.text: Some hours on a trip pay below 16 per hour on a trip (about a fifth).

a11.text: Buyers of shares and medallions expect the Act to survive the court challenge and repeal campaign.

a15.text: Some delivery services can operate with fewer than 100 Lanvik workers.

a17.text: Some workers exceed 40 hours a week with one company (about 600 on trips; about 5,000 logged in), and companies can cap them.

a18.text: Companies control dispatch enough to keep part-time employees' weekly wages at or under 150.

a19.text: Enforcement is imperfect: some misclassification and some pressure to sign occur.

a26.text: The Department's 4 million is new money from the general fund.

a28.text: §9 does not fix the fare share, and companies can cut fare shares and bonuses after launch.

a29.text: Fare shares are not cut in the first months (30 days' notice; scrutiny at launch).

a31.text: The floor's surplus of employee hours is rationed by stricter criteria than the counterfactual's dispatch ranking (shift allocation, acceptance thresholds).

j1.text: Many logged-in hours pay below 16 per logged-in hour (about three quarters).

j2.text: Some workers sign a contractor agreement.
